quote: Patients with unknown neuropathy 70 (Placebo/Ajwain as 36/34) … In regard of the neuropathic pain, previously established historical diagnosis as well as clinical examination such as nerve conduction studies was considered.
proposed_wording: No topical treatment has a positive randomised result in idiopathic small fibre neuropathy. The nearest is a randomised placebo-controlled trial of Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) cream in 92 patients enrolled on burning feet, 70 of them with neuropathy of unknown cause and 22 diabetic. It was positive on burning, but no small-fibre test was done and no result was reported by cause.
reason: The full text answers the open question. Aetiology was diabetic in 22 and 'unknown' in 70 (Table 2, p. 3), and the work-up was history plus clinical examination 'such as nerve conduction studies' (p. 2): no skin biopsy, QST or other small-fibre test. The sample also included patients with a history of stroke (21), multiple sclerosis (8), Parkinsonism or Alzheimer's (11) and radiculopathy (7), and the authors could not analyse by type of neuropathy (p. 6). So the trial overlaps idiopathic SFN only clinically, through burning feet of unknown cause, and gives no result in that subgroup; within the claim's scope (idiopathic SFN) it neither refutes nor narrows it.

quote: Due to the low sample size, we were unable to categorize types of neuropathy into detailed groups.
reason: The one randomised topical trial with a mixed diabetic and unknown-cause burning-feet population (Petramfar 2016) reports no response by aetiology: its authors say they could not split the sample by type of neuropathy. That population was not shown to be SFN, so the trial confirms the claim rather than touching its scope.

quote: Similar proportions of Cetomacrogol, Cetostearyl alcohol, Vaseline and Butylated hydroxytoluene were employed in Ajwain and placebo creams.
reason: The full text confirms that the burning-feet trial named as the nearest miss contained no menthol. The active was Ajwain seed essential oil (major constituents thymol, p-cymene, gamma-terpinene) and both creams shared a menthol-free base, so it is not a placebo-controlled trial of topical menthol with burning feet as the entry criterion.

quote: The pattern of quantitative sensory testing results for this patient led the authors to believe that she had an "irritable nociceptor" type of pathophysiology.
proposed_wording: That menthol at [dose figure omitted] is safe or unsafe specifically in a cold-hyperalgesic phenotype. No trial or series has phenotyped patients before treating them with it; one case report (Davies 2002) used quantitative sensory testing to class a patient with postherpetic neuralgia as an 'irritable nociceptor' type before treating her with peppermint oil, which contains menthol, and reports no cold-hyperalgesia subgroup or result.
reason: Found in Petramfar 2016's reference list (ref 29). Davies 2002 is a single case in postherpetic neuralgia: QST phenotyping came first and led the authors to treat with neat peppermint oil containing menthol, with pain relief and one minor side effect over 2 months. It matches 'phenotyped before treating', a neuropathic population and a menthol concentration inside the claim's range. It misses the cold-hyperalgesic subgroup (the phenotype named is 'irritable nociceptor') and the trial-or-series design, so the safety question stays open, but 'Nobody has phenotyped patients before treating them with it' is too broad. Page 0 = abstract.

quote: an observational cohort of 21 patients with established ATN (grade 0–4/4 by analgesic requirement, where 0 is asymptomatic, 1 is ATN but no analgesia required, 2 is ATN requiring non-opioid analgesics, 3 is opioid analgesics required, and 4 is pain uncontrolled by opioid analgesia) … Clinical grade of neuropathic pain improved in 15 of 21 patients overall
proposed_wording: No controlled trial of acetyl-L-carnitine has shown a structural and a pain benefit at the same dose. The one study in which both moved was an uncontrolled 21-patient HIV-neuropathy cohort (Hart 2004), and its symptom measure was a 0–4 grade set by analgesic requirement, not a pain score: it improved in 15 of 21 patients, with no statistical test reported and no analysis linking it to the skin results.
reason: Answer to the open question: pain was not measured on any pain scale. The 'neuropathic grade' is a 0–4 grade by analgesic requirement (p. 2). It improved in 15 of 21, was unchanged in 5 and worsened in 1 (p. 6; the abstract's '76% … 19%' does not match these counts). No test of the grade change and no correlation with the immunostaining results are reported, and skin was re-biopsied in only 16 at six months. The authors themselves say a randomised trial with a validated VAS is needed (p. 10). So Hart shows a structural signal and a crude analgesic-requirement signal together, uncontrolled. Within acetyl-L-carnitine the claim holds for controlled trials only, and the narrowing for the capsaicin patch trial outside ALC stands.

quote: Highly significant increases occurred in both epidermal (mean 100%; P = 0.006) and dermal (mean 133%; P < 0.0001) innervation after 6 months of ALCAR treatment
proposed_wording: Its only controlled structural results are sural myelinated fibre morphometry. Skin biopsies have been taken only in two uncontrolled HIV-neuropathy cohorts at twice the daily dose of the page's biopsy trial: one reported a rise in the immunostained area of small sensory (CGRP) fibres in epidermis and dermis (Hart 2004, 21 patients, 16 re-biopsied at six months), the other found no change in intraepidermal fibre counts (Valcour 2009, 21 patients). No controlled study has shown it touches the fibre type that burns.
reason: The full text confirms the refutation and sharpens it. The small-fibre result is CGRP immunostaining area in the epidermis and dermis (C and A-delta sensory fibres; p. 3, p. 7), not a fibre count. It rests on 16 patients biopsied at six months against 5 HIV-negative reference volunteers, with no control arm. 'Every structural result is sural myelinated morphometry' is false; 'never shown to touch the fibre type that burns' holds only for controlled evidence.

quote: While there was no placebo arm to this study, the natural history of untreated DSP suggests that the continuous and long-term beneficial effects found in this patient cohort resulted from ALCAR treatment.
reason: The full text confirms that Hart 2004 is not the study the claim says has never been done. It has no placebo arm, used excision biopsies (an ellipse of skin) rather than punch biopsies, and used 3,000 mg/day, not the 1,500 mg/day trial dose.

quote: fibre counts do not assess the health of surviving fibres, and atrophy or regeneration of fibres needs to be determined by immunostaining area quantification, as used in this study.
proposed_wording: Intraepidermal nerve fibre density is the standard objective measure of nerve loss in skin; sweat gland nerve fibre density, dermal fibre diameter, perivascular axon-Schwann ratios and quantified immunostaining area of epidermal, dermal and sweat-gland nerves are others, all requiring a biopsy.
reason: One more objective skin measure: Hart 2004 quantified the immunostaining area of PGP 9.5, CGRP and VIP fibres in epidermis, dermis and sweat glands under blinded image analysis, and cites earlier work relating such quantification to clinical neuropathy tests in diabetes and leprosy (refs 32–34). The claim's uniqueness wording stays refuted.

quote: Both male and female subjects between 18 and 70 years of age with a diagnosis of idiopathic SFN were included in this study.
proposed_wording: That anything on this page regenerates nerve in idiopathic small fibre neuropathy. One agent here has been tested in that population with a skin endpoint, and fibre density did not move: electrical stimulation of one leg for 60 days in eight people with idiopathic SFN, the other leg serving as an untreated control (Burakgazi 2020).
reason: The full text answers both parts of the open question. The subjects had idiopathic SFN: it is the inclusion criterion, and diabetes, abnormal HbA1c, vitamin deficiency, alcohol abuse and chemotherapy were excluded. The comparison was the subject's own contralateral leg, chosen by the subject, with no randomisation and no sham. That matches every element of 'no trial of any agent here has been run in that population with a skin endpoint': an agent on the page (electrical stimulation), idiopathic SFN, a prospective interventional study with an untreated control limb, and a skin (IENFD) endpoint. The first sentence still stands, since no regeneration was shown (1 of 8 grew).

quote: ENS therapy for this study was delivered to 1 leg using an AvivaStim XP stimulator, with the contralateral leg serving as an untreated control.
proposed_wording: Two structural device studies have been run in small fibre polyneuropathy: electrical stimulation of one leg in eight people with idiopathic SFN, the other leg untreated (no growth at 60 days), and an uncontrolled 19-patient spinal cord stimulation cohort of mixed causes, nine idiopathic, in which distal skin fibre density rose 22% at 12 months.
reason: The full text confirms the page's description (eight subjects, biopsies at 30 and 60 days, no meaningful growth; 1 of 8 grew) and adds that the population was idiopathic SFN and the control was each subject's untreated leg. The refutation itself rests on Canós-Verdecho 2025 and is unchanged.

quote: This study was sponsored by Research Acceleration Program of Carilion Clinic (intramural grant) Roanoke, VA.
reason: Settles the record's 'registration unknown' for Burakgazi 2020: the full text gives no trial registration, only an intramural grant and local IRB approval. So it is not a registered interventional trial and does not bear on 'first registered trial'. The refutation rests on the cibinetide and IVIG trials and is unchanged.

quote: Both male and female subjects between 18 and 70 years of age with a diagnosis of idiopathic SFN were included in this study.
proposed_wording: Burakgazi 2020, in eight people with idiopathic SFN, is one of only a handful of device studies in small fibre neuropathy, all small and uncontrolled: spinal cord stimulation with 12-month biopsies (Canós-Verdecho 2025, 19 patients), postural insoles (12 SFN patients), scrambler therapy, and case reports of spinal cord and DRG stimulation.
reason: The full text shows Burakgazi's population was idiopathic SFN, so 'this exact disease' fits it if the page means idiopathic SFN. The claim stays refuted because other device studies in SFN exist, one of them a case report of spinal cord stimulation in idiopathic SFN (Mohabbati 2024).

quote: ENS therapy for this study was delivered to 1 leg using an AvivaStim XP stimulator, with the contralateral leg serving as an untreated control.
proposed_wording: NCT07805057 would be the first sham-controlled device trial in skin-biopsy-proven idiopathic SFN; drugs have already been tested against placebo in this condition (IVIG, Geerts 2021, n=60, null; gabapentin and tramadol, Ho 2009; vixotrigine, CONVEY 2023), and one device has been tested without a sham, against an untreated leg (electrical stimulation, Burakgazi 2020, n=8, null).
reason: Burakgazi 2020 tested a device in idiopathic SFN with an untreated contralateral leg rather than a sham, so 'nothing in this condition has yet been tested' is wrong for devices too. 'First sham-controlled device trial' remains true. The paper does not say whether its subjects' SFN was biopsy-proven ('previously diagnosed SFN').

quote: Incorporating a dedicated measure of small caliber fiber such as skin biopsy was considered although ultimately not used due to the fact that regulatory authorities did not accept a change in this measure as a criterion for approval.
reason: Answer to the open question: the ranirestat phase II/III trial (NCT00927914, 800 randomised) did not include skin biopsy or IENFD among any of its endpoints. The authors say skin biopsy was considered and dropped because regulators did not accept it as an approval criterion, and they list the secondary and exploratory measures without it (p. 4). So this trial does not add to the class's skin-biopsy literature. The other half of the claim's uncertainty, what the 2000 letter is, is answered in the Yasuda 2000 entry (S-686-41).

quote: Nineteen patients were treated with epalrestat … for 13 months (ARI group) and 12 patients served as control subjects (control group).
proposed_wording: Its only fibre trial is a 2000 research letter: 19 patients with type 2 diabetic neuropathy on epalrestat for 13 months against 12 controls, with no randomisation or blinding described, measuring skin nerve fibre length by biopsy. Epidermal fibre length did not change and dermal fibre length rose (Yasuda 2000). It has no randomised fibre-density trial.
reason: The full text answers the open question. The agent was epalrestat; there was a control group (12, not stated to be randomised or placebo); and cutaneous nerve fibre length, a skin fibre-quantity measure from PGP 9.5 biopsies, was the treatment outcome over 13 months. That matches the claim's population (diabetic neuropathy), intervention, design (a controlled trial) and outcome (skin fibre measure), so 'no fibre-density trial' is refuted. The result was null in the epidermis, the layer IENFD counts, and positive only in the dermis.

quote: Using this technique, we evaluated the therapeutic effect of aldose reductase inhibitor (ARI) epalrestat in 32 type 2 diabetic patients with neuropathy.
proposed_wording: The entire skin-biopsy literature for this class in the marketed era is a single 2000 research letter in Diabetes Care, published without an abstract: 19 patients on epalrestat against 12 controls for 13 months, dermal nerve fibre length up and epidermal unchanged.
reason: The letter is the epalrestat skin-biopsy study the claim describes (agent, journal, year and letter format all confirmed), and Polydefkis 2015 (S-686-22) shows that the 800-patient ranirestat trial took no skin biopsies. Nothing found extends the class's skin literature, so the claim stands; the added wording only says what the letter contains.

quote: We reported that dermal nerve fiber length (NFL), which was obtained by measuring nerve fiber PGP 9.5, immunostained, and labeled with streptavidin fluorescein isothiocyanate under confocal laser scanning microscopy, was significantly shorter in diabetic patients than in control subjects (2).
reason: One more objective skin measure besides intraepidermal fibre density: dermal and epidermal nerve fibre length by confocal PGP 9.5 immunofluorescence, shorter in diabetes and used as a treatment outcome. The claim stays refuted (see also the Hart 2004 entry).

quote: Intradermal administration with [dose figure omitted] of BTX-A or normal saline solution (placebo) … Double-blind crossover trial of intradermal BTX-A for diabetic neuropathic pain
proposed_wording: Wang C, Zhang Q, Wang R, Xu L. … — The largest pooled analysis whose trials were all intradermal: four randomized trials, 231 patients. Its abstract gives no route criterion; every trial it found was intradermal. An earlier meta-analysis, Lakhan 2015 (Pain Medicine, PMID 25800040), pooled two randomized placebo-controlled trials in painful diabetic neuropathy, Yuan 2009 and Ghasemi 2014, both intradermal (58 patients), to a VAS difference of −1.96 (95% CI −3.09 to −0.84).
reason: Answer to the open question. Lakhan pooled exactly two trials: Yuan 2009 (Neurology, PMID 19246421; double-blind crossover, onabotulinumtoxinA, 18 analysed) and Ghasemi 2014 (J Res Med Sci, PMID 24778662; double-blind parallel, abobotulinumtoxinA, 40 patients). Its Table 2 describes both as intradermal, into the dorsum of the foot (p. 3), and the results restate the shared grid (p. 6). A third trial, Chen 2013 (PMID 23462284), was excluded as a duplicate report of Yuan. Route was not an inclusion criterion: the review took AAN class I/II double-blind placebo-controlled trials in painful diabetic neuropathy (pp. 2, 5). Wang 2021's abstract does not give one either ('RCTs were included if they were related to the treatment of DPN pain with BTX-A'). Both reviews are therefore restricted to the intradermal route in the same sense, by what they found, and Wang's is not the only one. Lakhan adds no trial that Wang 2021 and the Notion pages do not already cover: Ghasemi is cited on the botulinum page and both trials in Reference S150. Its pooled estimate also counts the crossover patients in both arms (58 patients, 76 treatments).

quote: In our study, patients who received unilateral BTX-A injections showed decreased VAS score in both feet, which may reflect the central effects of BTX-A injection (and not just the topical effect).
proposed_wording: Whether the crossover to the untreated side is large enough to halve the dose needed is unstudied. A third of patients injected in one foot reported relief in both, pooled analysis found no significant difference between one-foot and two-foot injection, and a three-arm randomised trial that gave each patient the same total amount — all of it in one foot in one arm, divided between both feet in the other — found the two arms differed on only one of ten items, hot sensation, which improved less when the amount was split across both feet. What none of them tests is a smaller total.
reason: Answer to the open question, in two parts. (1) The saline-injected foot of the one-foot group is not reported separately: the visual analogue scale and all ten Neuropathy Pain Scale items were recorded per patient, not per foot, and the trial's only statement about the untreated side is the Discussion sentence quoted here, with no count of patients and no figure. So this trial is not a second measurement of the untreated foot; it is a second author group reporting the same impression. (2) The bilateral arm's amount was per patient, not per foot: 'For each patient, total of [dose figure omitted] of BTX- A was injected' (p. 2), with that total divided equally between the two feet in the bilateral arm, so the per-foot amount there was half the unilateral arm's while the per-patient total matched. That makes this a randomised head-to-head of one foot against both at a matched total, and the arms separated on only one item (hot sensation, improving less in the bilateral arm, p=0.003, p. 3). The verdict stays narrowed because the dose-halving question itself is still untested: no arm received a smaller total.

quote: When comparing group D1 and D2, only hot sensation showed a significant difference; in other words, hot sensation improvement was significantly lower among those patients who received injection in both feet compared to one foot
proposed_wording: So one of three things has to give: the area treated, the density of the grid, or the units delivered per point. One randomised trial has varied two of them deliberately: holding the total per patient and the grid geometry fixed, it compared all of the toxin in one foot against the same total divided between both feet, which halves the amount per point and doubles the area. The two arms separated on one of ten items — hot sensation, which improved less when the amount was spread across both feet. What has not been varied deliberately is the density of the grid, or the fraction of a single painful region covered.
reason: Taheri 2020 is a randomised, double-blind, three-arm trial that deliberately varied the treated area and the amount delivered per point while holding the per-patient total and the grid geometry constant (one foot against both feet, p. 2), with pain as the outcome. That matches every element of the claim — population, intervention, design, outcome — so 'none has varied them deliberately' is refuted, as is the later sentence that 'no trial has varied it deliberately'. The result is also informative rather than null: of ten items only hot sensation differed, and it favoured concentrating the amount in one foot (p=0.003, p. 3). Grid density was not varied, and no trial has covered part of one painful region, so the page's underlying worry survives in narrower form. Verdict was already narrowed on the abstract; the full text confirms the deliberate variation and adds the direction of the one difference.

quote: It is of note that the total injected volume for each patient in each group was equal to [dose figure omitted].
reason: Checked and unchanged. This randomised controlled trial states an amount per injection point and a spacing between points, but no units-per-area figure, so the claim as worded still holds for controlled trials; the per-area number remains a derivation, here from a trial's geometry rather than from a sentence in it. The narrowing already recorded (one uncontrolled study dosed explicitly by area) is unaffected. Figures not recorded here, per the dose rule.

quote: In this study, we present molecular dynamics simulations of the open-activated pore-domain of TRPV1 in the presence of three cationic species: Na+, … Ca2+ and K+.
proposed_wording: The pore diameters in 3.4.3 have a source and one of them is wrong. The cryo-EM structure paper (Cao 2013, Nature 504:113–118) measures the lower gate in three states: closed, it is a hydrophobic seal about 5 Å across, too narrow for hydrated ions rather than for bare ions; with capsaicin it widens to about 8 Å; fully open, with resiniferatoxin and a spider toxin, to about 9 Å. The 'about 10 Å open' figure is close to that last number; the 'about 1 Å closed' figure corresponds to nothing in the paper and should be replaced, with the structure paper cited.
reason: Answer to the open question, in two steps. The paper flagged for full text, Darré 2015, cannot supply either figure: it is a molecular dynamics study of the open-activated state alone, built on PDB 3J5Q, with S1–S4 and the intracellular domain removed and the intracellular gate restrained open, so it has no closed-state geometry at all (pp. 2, 4, 12). The only pore dimension it prints is the diameter of an ion binding site inside the selectivity filter, about 8 Å, which is not the gate (p. 11) and is easy to mistake for an open-pore diameter. The figures belong instead to the structure paper Darré is built on, Cao 2013 (PMID 24305161, PMC4023639), whose full text gives the lower gate as a 5.3 Å hydrophobic seal when closed, 7.6 Å with capsaicin and 9.3 Å fully open, and the selectivity filter widening from 4.6 to 7.6 Å at its narrowest point. So a structure paper does report these pore dimensions — the claim that the figures are given without one available is refuted — and attaching it corrects the closed figure from about 1 Å to about 5 Å.
